lessons.title: A framework for system design interviews
lessons.summary: A repeatable seven-step method for a 45-minute design interview, how to spend the time, what interviewers actually score, and the mistakes that sink candidates.
lessons.body:
A system design interview is not a test of whether you know the "right" architecture for Twitter. There isn't one. It is a test of whether you can take a vague problem, turn it into a concrete one, and reason your way to a design that works, while explaining your trade-offs out loud.

That means *process* matters as much as knowledge. Candidates with encyclopaedic knowledge still fail because they jump straight to drawing Kafka boxes. Candidates with modest knowledge pass because they ask good questions, size the problem, and make each decision for a stated reason.

This lesson proposes a practice framework, not a universal hiring rubric. Timings, seniority signals and suggested answers vary by employer and interviewer; use the actual interview brief. This lesson gives you a method. Every case study in this module follows it, so you can see it applied six times.

## The shape of the interview

For practice, assume a design round of 45 to 60 minutes. Take off five minutes of introductions and five of your questions at the end and you have about 35 to 45 minutes of actual design. That is not long. The single biggest failure mode is running out of time with half a design on the board.

A reasonable budget for a 45-minute slot:

| Step | Minutes |
|---|---|
| 1. Requirements | 5 |
| 2. Estimates | 3–5 |
| 3. API | 3–5 |
| 4. Data model | 3–5 |
| 5. High-level design | 8–10 |
| 6. Deep dives | 10–15 |
| 7. Wrap-up | 2–3 |

The ranges add up to 34–48 minutes, so in a 45-minute slot you will be at the bottom of most of them. These aren't rigid. A senior candidate should spend *less* time on steps 1–5 and more on deep dives, because that's where seniority shows.

## Step 1: Clarify requirements

The prompt is deliberately vague: "Design a URL shortener." Your first job is to pin it down. Split requirements into two kinds.

**Functional requirements** are what the system does, phrased as user actions:

- Users can create a short link from a long URL.
- Visiting the short link redirects to the long URL.
- Users can optionally pick a custom alias.
- Links can expire.

**Non-functional requirements** are the qualities the system must have:

- Scale: how many users, requests per second, how much data?
- Latency: redirects under ~50 ms at p99?
- Availability vs consistency: is it worse to be down or to be briefly stale?
- Durability: can we ever lose a link? (No.)

Write them on the board. Then explicitly scope out what you won't do: "I'll skip user accounts and billing unless you want them." Interviewers like this; it shows you can prioritise.

> [!tip] Ask, then propose
> Don't interrogate the interviewer with twenty questions. Ask the three or four that change the design ("Is this read-heavy?", "Global or one region?"), then *propose* sensible defaults for the rest and ask if they're OK.

## Step 2: Back-of-the-envelope estimates

Estimates tell you which problems are real. A write count alone does not determine capacity: transaction complexity, indexes, contention, durability, hardware and latency targets matter. Don't compute to three significant figures. Round aggressively and keep powers of ten.

Numbers worth memorising:

- 1 day = 86,400 s ≈ **10^5 s** (use 100k for mental maths; it understates rates by 13.6%, which rarely matters).
- 1 million requests/day ≈ **12 per second**. 1 billion/day ≈ 12,000/s.
- Use **2–3x** as an explicit illustrative peak assumption if no traffic profile is supplied; campaigns and diurnal skew can produce much higher ratios.
- 1 million × 1 KB = 1 GB; 1 billion × 1 KB = 1 TB. Most storage sums reduce to this.

> [!note] Content gap: universal capacity and latency numbers
> No reproducible benchmark supports a universal database writes/s, Redis operations/s, app-server throughput or hardware/network latency for this scenario. Those values are omitted. Use measured workload capacity or explicitly supplied hypothetical inputs when sizing.

A worked example, for a service with 100M daily active users who each make 10 reads and 1 write per day:

```
Writes: 100M x 1 / 10^5 s  = 1,000/s
Reads:  100M x 10 / 10^5 s = 10,000/s
Peak (x3): 3k writes/s, 30k reads/s
Storage: 100M writes/day x 1 KB
       = 100 GB/day = ~36 TB/year
```

(Dividing by the exact 86,400 gives about 1,160 writes/s and 11,600 reads/s; the shortcut is close enough.)

Now you know: reads dominate 10:1 (cache them), 3k writes/s is a target to test against the chosen primary (and a partitioning strategy is useful if tests reveal a limit), and storage grows by tens of terabytes a year.

Say what the numbers *imply*. "36 TB a year, nearly 200 TB over five years before replication, requires a storage, backup and recovery plan; I will evaluate partitioning, tiering and sharding against those constraints" is worth far more than the arithmetic itself.

> [!example] From QPS to machines
> Divide peak load by what one unit handles, then add headroom. 30k reads/s at peak with a 90% cache hit rate leaves 3k reads/s for the database: the required replica count still depends on measured query capacity. If each app server handles an assumed 1,000 req/s, 33k total requests/s needs ~35 servers, with three evenly sized zones, 54 servers leave 36 after losing one zone, above the rounded 35-server requirement. Add further headroom for deploys, uneven traffic and measurement error.

## Step 3: API design

Define the contract between clients and your system. Usually a handful of REST endpoints is enough:

```
POST /v1/links  {longUrl, alias?, ttl?}
  -> 201 {shortUrl}
GET  /{code}    -> 302 Location: longUrl
```

Things to mention: authentication (API keys or OAuth tokens), pagination (cursor-based, not offset), idempotency keys for writes that might be retried, and rate limits. For real-time features say *how* the client connects (WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, long polling) and why.

## Step 4: Data model

Name the core entities, their key fields and, crucially, the **access patterns**: what you look up by what. The access pattern drives the choice of store and the partition key.

- "Look up a link by its short code" means a key-value lookup; any store works, and the partition key is the code.
- "Get a user's last 50 messages in a conversation" means a range scan ordered by time within a partition; a wide-column store such as Cassandra with partition key `conversation_id` and clustering key `message_id` fits well.

Justify SQL vs NoSQL by the access pattern and scale, not by fashion. "Relational, because we need transactions across the order and payment tables" is a good reason. "NoSQL because it scales" is not.

## Step 5: High-level design

Draw the boxes and arrows that satisfy the functional requirements end to end. Start simple:

```
 Client
   |
   v
 Load balancer
   |
   v
 App servers (stateless) --> Cache
   |
   v
 Database (primary + replicas)
```

Then walk a request through it: "A redirect hits the load balancer, an app server checks Redis, on a miss reads the database, and returns a 302." Walking requests through the diagram catches gaps (where does the ID come from?) before the interviewer does.

Only add components when a requirement or an estimate demands them. Every box should have a reason. A message queue appears because you need to absorb bursts or decouple a slow step, not because big systems have queues.

## Step 6: Deep dives

This is where you earn the senior rating. Pick the two or three hardest parts of *this* problem and go deep:

- URL shortener: unique ID generation without coordination.
- Chat: delivering to a user connected to a different server.
- News feed: the celebrity with 100M followers.

Often the interviewer will steer you here. If they don't, choose yourself: "The interesting part is fan-out; shall I go deep on that?"

For each deep dive, show **options and trade-offs**, then choose. "We could hash the URL, use a counter, or use Snowflake IDs. Hashing needs collision handling; a counter needs coordination; Snowflake needs clock discipline. I'll use a counter with range allocation because..."

Also cover failure: what happens when this node dies, this region goes dark, this queue backs up? Senior engineers think about failure modes by reflex.

A useful checklist of probes that come up in almost every design, so you can raise them before you're asked:

- **Hot keys and skew**: one celebrity, one viral link, one huge group chat.
- **Retries and duplicates**: what is idempotent, and where is the dedup key?
- **Consistency**: which reads can be stale, and for how long?
- **Backpressure**: what happens when a downstream dependency is slow, and does the queue grow without bound?
- **Fail-open or fail-closed**: when a dependency is down, do you allow the request or reject it?
- **Multi-region**: where do writes go, and what does a user see after a regional failover?

## Step 7: Wrap up and evolve

Spend the last few minutes on:

- **Bottlenecks**: what breaks first as load grows?
- **10x scale**: what would you change? (Shard further, add regions, move to async processing.)
- **Operational concerns**: monitoring, alerting, deployment, data migration.
- **Cost**: at staff level, say which component dominates the bill (often storage or egress) and one way to cut it.

Finish with a one-sentence summary of the design and its key trade-off. It leaves the interviewer with a clear picture to write up.

## A practice review checklist

Use these dimensions as a practice checklist; they are not asserted to be the scorecard of most companies:

1. **Problem navigation**: did you clarify scope, or charge off in a random direction?
2. **Solution design**: does the design actually work end to end and meet the requirements?
3. **Technical depth**: can you go deep on at least a couple of components (database internals, consistency, caching behaviour)?
4. **Trade-offs**: do you articulate alternatives and *why* you chose one?
5. **Communication**: can the interviewer follow your reasoning? Do you respond well to hints?

Seniority changes the bar. A mid-level candidate is expected to produce a working design with some guidance. A senior candidate drives the conversation, identifies the hard parts unprompted, and discusses failure modes. A staff candidate also talks about evolution, operability, cost and organisational trade-offs.

## Common mistakes

- **Jumping to the solution.** Drawing Kafka in minute two, before you know whether the system does 10 writes per second or 10 million.
- **Over-engineering.** Microservices, three caches and a service mesh for a system that fits on one database. Scale the design to the numbers.
- **Buzzword architecture.** Naming technologies without saying what they do for this problem. "I'll use Cassandra" means nothing without "because the access pattern is a partitioned time-ordered range scan and we need high write throughput".
- **Ignoring the interviewer.** If they ask "what about hot keys?" it's a hint, not small talk.
- **Silent thinking.** The interviewer can only score what they hear. Think out loud.
- **Not finishing.** A complete simple design beats a half-finished elaborate one. Get end to end first, then deepen.
- **Pretending.** If you don't know how something works, say so and reason from first principles. Bluffing is easy to spot.

> [!warning] Estimates are a tool, not a ritual
> Some candidates spend ten minutes on estimates and then never refer to them again. Only compute numbers that will change a decision, and then use them.

## Key takeaways

- Follow a fixed sequence: requirements, estimates, API, data model, high-level design, deep dives, wrap-up.
- Split requirements into functional (what it does) and non-functional (scale, latency, availability, durability), and scope things out explicitly.
- Round estimates to powers of ten; 1M requests/day ≈ 12/s and 1B × 1 KB = 1 TB. Always state what each number implies.
- Turn estimates into machine counts (peak load ÷ per-unit capacity, plus headroom) to decide what needs to scale out.
- Let access patterns choose the data store and partition key.
- Get a simple end-to-end design on the board before going deep.
- Spend most time on the two or three genuinely hard parts, showing alternatives and failure modes.
- Interviewers score navigation, design, depth, trade-offs and communication; seniority is shown by driving the conversation.

- [Tech Interview Handbook: system design](https://www.techinterviewhandbook.org/system-design/)
- [Hello Interview: a delivery framework for system design](https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/delivery)

questions.prompt: The interviewer says: "Design Instagram." What should you do in the first five minutes?

options.text: Draw the high-level architecture with a CDN, object store and feed service, since those are needed for any photo app.
options.explanation: Wrong. Drawing components before you know the scope and scale is the classic 'jumping to the solution' mistake. You don't yet know whether the feed, stories, DMs or search are in scope, or whether this is 1,000 or 1 billion users.

options.text: Ask the interviewer which database they would like you to use.
options.explanation: Wrong. Technology choices are yours to make and justify from the access patterns. Asking the interviewer to pick hands away the very decision they want to see you reason about.

options.text: Compute detailed storage estimates to three significant figures so the interviewer sees your rigour.
options.explanation: Wrong. Estimates come after you know what you are building, and precision beyond an order of magnitude wastes time. Interviewers want rounded numbers that drive decisions, not arithmetic theatre.

options.text: Clarify functional requirements (upload, feed, follow), agree non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability) and explicitly scope out features you'll skip.
options.explanation: Correct. Turning a vague prompt into a concrete, agreed problem is the first thing interviewers score ('problem navigation'). It also stops you designing features nobody asked for.

questions.workedExample:
Think of the first five minutes as converting the prompt into a spec.

1. **Functional**: list user actions. "Users upload photos; follow others; see a feed of people they follow."
2. **Non-functional**: ask the questions that change the design. "How many DAU? Read-heavy? Global?" Propose defaults: "Say 500M DAU, feed p99 under 200 ms, availability over consistency for the feed."
3. **Out of scope**: "I'll skip DMs, stories and ads unless you want them."

Only now do you know enough to estimate and draw.

questions.prompt: A service receives **50 million requests per day**. Roughly what is the average request rate per second?

options.text: About 500–600 per second
options.explanation: Correct. 50 million / 86,400 s ≈ 580/s. Using the 10^5 shortcut gives 500/s, close enough for design decisions.

options.text: About 6,000 per second
options.explanation: Wrong. 6,000/s would be about 500 million requests a day. Check the division: 50M / 100k = 500, not 6,000.

options.text: About 50 per second
options.explanation: Wrong. This is off by an order of magnitude: you would get 50/s from about 4–5 million requests a day.

options.text: About 50,000 per second
options.explanation: Wrong. That would be about 4.3 billion requests per day. This mistake usually comes from dividing by 1,000 (seconds in ~17 minutes) instead of by 86,400.

questions.workedExample:
Use the shortcut **1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds**.

```
50,000,000 / 100,000 = 500 req/s
Exact: 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 579 req/s
```

With an explicitly assumed 2–3x peak factor and the rounded 500/s baseline, plan for **1,000–1,500 req/s**. Measure the workload before deciding server count; request rate alone does not prove that a particular database or fleet is sufficient.

A handy anchor: **1M/day ≈ 12/s**, so 50M/day ≈ 50 × 12 = 600/s.

questions.prompt: You estimate your system will store **2 KB per record** and receive **20 million new records per day**, kept for **5 years**. What does that imply?

options.text: About 730 GB in total, so it fits in memory on a single cache node.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is two orders of magnitude too low. It is a common slip when converting GB/day to a yearly total (multiplying by 36.5 instead of 365) and dropping the 5 years.

options.text: About 7 TB in total, which fits comfortably on one large Postgres server.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is an order of magnitude too low: it is roughly what you'd store with 2 million records a day. Also forgetting replicas (usually 3x) and index overhead makes the real footprint even larger.

options.text: About 73 TB in total, which requires an explicit storage, recovery and growth plan; evaluate partitioning, tiering or sharding.
options.explanation: Correct. 20M × 2 KB = 40 GB/day; × 365 ≈ 14.6 TB/year; × 5 ≈ 73 TB, before replication and indexes. It is not a universal single-node limit; feasible storage size and recovery objectives depend on the deployment.

options.text: Storage isn't worth estimating; you should only estimate QPS.
options.explanation: Wrong. Storage often decides the data layer: whether you need sharding, tiered storage, or an object store. Skipping it means you might design a single-node database for a 73 TB dataset.

questions.workedExample:
Step by step:

```
Per day:  20M x 2 KB   = 40 GB
Per year: 40 GB x 365  ≈ 14.6 TB
5 years:  14.6 x 5     ≈ 73 TB
With 3x replication    ≈ 220 TB
```

The implication is what you say out loud: "About 70 TB of raw data, over 200 TB replicated. I would evaluate sharding and backup/recovery costs, and I'd consider moving records older than a year to cheaper object storage."

questions.prompt: Which of these are **non-functional** requirements? Select all that apply.

options.text: Redirects must complete in under 50 ms at p99.
options.explanation: Correct. Latency is a quality of the system, not a feature a user performs.

options.text: Users can set a custom alias for a short link.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a functional requirement: a specific capability the user invokes.

options.text: The system must tolerate the loss of one availability zone without downtime.
options.explanation: Correct. Availability and fault tolerance describe how well the system works, not what it does.

options.text: Once created, a link must never be lost.
options.explanation: Correct. Durability is a non-functional requirement. It pushes you towards replicated, persistent storage rather than cache-only.

options.text: Users can see how many times their link has been clicked.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Viewing click counts is a feature (functional). How fresh those counts must be would be the non-functional part.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each statement: "Is this something a user *does*, or a property of *how well* the system does it?"

- Custom alias, view click counts: user actions, so **functional**.
- p99 latency, AZ failure tolerance, never losing data: properties of the system, so **non-functional**.

Non-functional requirements are usually what make a design hard. Any intern can build a URL shortener; building one that does 100k redirects/s at 50 ms p99 across regions is the interview.

questions.prompt: Twenty minutes in, you have a high-level design. The interviewer asks: "What happens if one of your cache nodes holds a key that gets 200,000 reads a second?" How should you treat this?

options.text: As small talk; acknowledge it and move on to finishing your diagram.
options.explanation: Wrong. Interviewer questions are almost always hints pointing at a weakness they want you to address. Brushing them off loses points on both communication and technical depth.

options.text: Restart the design using a different database that doesn't need a cache.
options.explanation: Wrong. Throwing away a working design in response to a localised problem wastes time and suggests you can't reason incrementally. Hot keys are solved inside the caching layer.

options.text: Say that the cache will auto-scale, so this can't be a problem.
options.explanation: Wrong. Adding nodes doesn't help a single hot key: consistent hashing still maps that key to one node. This answer reveals a misunderstanding of how partitioned caches work.

options.text: As a hint about a hot-key problem: explain the failure (one node saturates) and propose mitigations such as replicating hot keys, a local in-process cache, or key splitting.
options.explanation: Correct. The interviewer is steering you into a deep dive. Name the failure mode, offer options with trade-offs, and choose one.

questions.workedExample:
Recognise the pattern: a pointed "what happens if..." question means the interviewer has spotted something.

1. **Name the problem**: a single key hashes to one cache node; 200k reads/s may saturate that node; establish its actual limit using a representative benchmark.
2. **Options**:
   - Replicate the key to N nodes and read from a random replica (`key#1`..`key#N`).
   - Add a small in-process LRU cache on each app server with a short TTL.
   - Put a CDN in front if the response is cacheable.
3. **Choose**: "I'd add a local cache with a 5-second TTL; it absorbs most of the load and the staleness is acceptable here."

questions.prompt: Your estimates show **200 writes/s** and **2,000 reads/s** at peak, with 500 GB of data after three years. Assume a benchmark shows this workload meets its latency and recovery targets on one relational primary with a replica and cache. A candidate proposes microservices, Kafka, Cassandra and a Redis cluster. What is the best critique?

options.text: It's fine; interviewers reward using as many technologies as possible.
options.explanation: Wrong. Interviewers penalise over-engineering. Every component adds operational cost and failure modes, and adding them without a requirement that demands them shows poor judgement.

options.text: Cassandra is wrong because it can't handle 200 writes/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cassandra handles far more than 200 writes/s; the issue is not capacity but that it's unnecessary at this scale and gives up relational features you might want.

options.text: The load fits a single relational primary with a read replica and a modest cache; the extra components add cost and failure modes without solving a real problem at these numbers.
options.explanation: Correct. The prompt explicitly supplies a successful benchmark for the simpler design. Scale the design to the numbers and say what would trigger adding more.

options.text: It needs a second Kafka cluster for redundancy.
options.explanation: Wrong. This doubles down on the problem. Nothing in the requirements needs a log-based message broker at all, let alone two.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the load against what simple components handle:

| Load | Simple capacity |
|---|---|
| 200 writes/s | Primary passes stated benchmark |
| 2,000 reads/s | Replica + cache pass benchmark |
| 500 GB | Fits on one node's SSD |

Nothing here forces sharding or a distributed log. The senior answer is: "Start with Postgres plus a replica and Redis. If measured write capacity becomes the limit, I would evaluate sharding by user ID; if we need async processing I'd add a queue then." Showing the *trigger* for each addition is what separates judgement from buzzwords.

questions.prompt: You're interviewing for a **senior** role. Which behaviours most distinguish a senior performance from a mid-level one? Select all that apply.

options.text: Identifying the hardest parts of the problem unprompted and proposing to deep-dive on them.
options.explanation: Correct. Driving the conversation towards what matters, rather than waiting to be led, is a core senior signal.

options.text: Discussing failure modes (node loss, region failure, backlog) and how the design degrades.
options.explanation: Correct. Seniors reason about what breaks and how the system behaves when it does, not just the happy path.

options.text: Naming more technologies than the other candidates.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Breadth of buzzwords isn't depth. Interviewers look for justified choices, and unexplained technology names count against you.

options.text: Presenting alternatives and explaining why one was chosen for these requirements.
options.explanation: Correct. Articulating trade-offs is one of the main scored dimensions and is expected far more strongly at senior level.

options.text: Spending the first 15 minutes on precise capacity calculations.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Over-investing in estimates leaves no time for deep dives, where seniority actually shows. Rounded numbers that drive decisions are enough.

questions.workedExample:
Map each behaviour onto the scoring dimensions:

- **Driving the hard parts** → problem navigation and depth.
- **Failure modes** → depth and operational maturity.
- **Trade-offs** → explicitly scored.
- **More technologies** → no dimension rewards this; it often hurts.
- **Long precise estimates** → wastes the deep-dive budget.

A practical rule: by minute 20 of 45 you should be in deep dives. If you aren't, you've spent too long on the early steps.

questions.prompt: Peak load is **40,000 requests/s**. Each stateless app server handles about **1,000 requests/s** at a safe CPU level, and you run across three availability zones. Roughly how many app servers should you provision?

options.text: 40, exactly peak divided by per-server capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. That leaves zero headroom: lose one zone (a third of the fleet) or roll a deploy and the survivors are overloaded at peak.

options.text: About 60, so that losing any one of three zones still leaves 40 servers.
options.explanation: Correct. With 20 per zone, losing a zone leaves 40 servers, exactly enough for peak. Many teams add a further margin for deploys and traffic growth.

options.text: About 400, because you should always provision 10x peak.
options.explanation: Wrong. 10x is wasteful and has no basis. Headroom should be sized to a specific failure (a zone loss, a deploy wave) plus expected growth.

options.text: 4, because servers can autoscale during peaks.
options.explanation: Wrong. Autoscaling helps with gradual growth, but it reacts in minutes and still needs the capacity to exist. Four servers would serve a tenth of peak.

questions.workedExample:
Size for peak, then for the failure you must survive.

```
Needed at peak: 40,000 / 1,000 = 40
Survive 1 of 3 zones down:
  40 / (2/3) = 60 servers
  = 20 per zone
```

Saying this out loud shows the interviewer you think about failure while sizing, not after. You'd then add: "plus some slack for deploys, so maybe 66–70".

questions.prompt: In a design for a ride-hailing app, the main query is: "find available drivers within 2 km of this point, many times per second". A candidate says: "I'll use Postgres because it's reliable." What is missing from the justification?

options.text: Nothing; reliability is the most important property of any database.
options.explanation: Wrong. Reliability is necessary but says nothing about whether the store fits the access pattern. Almost every mainstream database is reliable.

options.text: They should have chosen MongoDB, because NoSQL always scales better.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swapping one unjustified choice for another doesn't fix the reasoning. 'NoSQL scales' is exactly the fashion-driven argument to avoid.

options.text: The access pattern: a frequently updated geospatial proximity query. The choice should say how that is served, for example a geospatial index (PostGIS, geohash keys) or an in-memory spatial index.
options.explanation: Correct. The data model step is about access patterns. Naming the query shape and how the store serves it (and at what update rate) is what makes the choice defensible.

options.text: The number of tables the schema will need.
options.explanation: Wrong. Table count isn't a design driver. The shape and frequency of queries and writes are.

questions.workedExample:
Work from the access pattern outwards:

1. **Query**: nearby drivers for a point, read-heavy and latency-sensitive.
2. **Writes**: every active driver sends a location every few seconds, so a high, constantly changing write rate.
3. **Fit**: a geospatial index (PostGIS, or geohash-prefixed keys in Redis) answers proximity; very frequent location updates may favour an in-memory store over a durable one.

A good answer: "Driver locations go in an in-memory geo index, since they're ephemeral and updated constantly; trips and payments go in Postgres because they need transactions."

questions.prompt: You're writing the API for a payments-style endpoint, `POST /v1/transfers`, that mobile clients call over flaky networks, plus `GET /v1/transfers` to list a user's history. Which details are worth stating? Select all that apply.

options.text: An idempotency key on the POST, so a retried request after a timeout doesn't create a second transfer.
options.explanation: Correct. On a flaky network the client can't tell whether a timed-out request succeeded. An idempotency key lets the server return the original result instead of executing twice.

options.text: Cursor-based pagination on the GET, rather than page numbers with offsets.
options.explanation: Correct. Offsets are slow on large tables and skip or repeat items when new rows arrive. Keyset pagination needs a stable total order, matching cursor and suitable index; a cursor alone does not guarantee snapshot consistency.

options.text: Authentication on both endpoints, for example OAuth bearer tokens.
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson lists authentication as a standard API-step mention, and for money movement it is non-negotiable.

options.text: The exact JSON field names for every response, written out in full.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Field-level detail eats time and earns little. A sketch of the main fields is enough; spend the minutes on behaviour like idempotency.

options.text: Making the GET endpoint use POST so it can't be cached.
options.explanation: Incorrect. POST can implement a query and can sometimes be cached; changing the method does not guarantee non-caching. For this simple retrieval use GET with appropriate Cache-Control.

questions.workedExample:
For each API detail ask: "does this change correctness or scalability?"

- **Idempotency key**: prevents double transfers on retry, so it's about correctness.
- **Cursor pagination**: keeps listing fast and stable as the table grows, so it's about scalability and correctness.
- **Auth**: security baseline.
- **Exact field names**: no design impact.
- **Wrong verb**: makes things worse.

A compact way to say it:

```
POST /v1/transfers
  Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
GET  /v1/transfers?cursor=..&limit=50
```

questions.prompt: It's minute 30 of 45. You've finished requirements, estimates, API and data model in great detail, but your high-level diagram is half-drawn and you haven't started a deep dive. What's the best recovery?

options.text: Keep refining the data model, since a perfect schema is what interviewers value most.
options.explanation: Wrong. Interviewers score whether the design works end to end. A beautiful schema attached to an unfinished design still fails 'solution design'.

options.text: Say you're conscious of time, quickly complete a simple end-to-end design, walk one request through it, then pick the single hardest problem for a focused deep dive.
options.explanation: Correct. A complete simple design beats a half-finished elaborate one. Naming the time pressure shows self-awareness, and one good deep dive is better than none.

options.text: Ask the interviewer for an extra 15 minutes.
options.explanation: Wrong. The slot is fixed and the interviewer has to score what they saw. Managing the clock is part of what's being assessed.

Triage like an engineer under a deadline:

1. **Acknowledge**: "I've spent too long on the early steps; let me get end to end."
2. **Finish the skeleton** (5 min): client → LB → stateless services → cache → store.
3. **Walk one request** through it to prove it works.

link.title: Hello Interview: a delivery framework for system design

questions.prompt: In wrap-up for a **staff** role, the interviewer asks: "This is live and traffic grows 10x over a year. What do you do?" Assume load tests identify the primary as the first bottleneck at 3x load and projected storage dominates costs. Which answer best addresses the stated evidence?

options.text: "Add more servers."
options.explanation: Wrong. Stateless tiers do scale by adding servers, but this ignores the components that don't (the database primary, hot keys) and says nothing about cost or risk.

options.text: "Rewrite everything as microservices on Kubernetes."
options.explanation: Wrong. A rewrite is a huge organisational risk and doesn't target a specific bottleneck. Staff engineers change the smallest thing that removes the actual constraint.

options.text: "The write path on the single primary breaks first, at about 3x. I'd introduce sharding by user ID behind the data-access layer and migrate with a durable change stream or outbox, backfill, reconciliation and controlled cutover. Cache and app tiers scale horizontally. Storage cost grows fastest, so I'd tier cold data to object storage. I'd add load-test and capacity alerts so we see the next limit early."
options.explanation: Correct. It names the first bottleneck with a number, gives a migration path rather than a big bang, addresses cost and operations, and plans for finding the next limit.

options.text: "10x is too speculative to plan for; I'd wait and see."
options.explanation: Wrong. Ignoring the question avoids the evolution discussion that the staff bar specifically looks for.

questions.workedExample:
A strong evolution answer has four parts:

1. **First bottleneck, quantified**: which component saturates and at what multiple of today's load.
2. **Change with a migration plan**: how to get there without downtime (durable change capture, backfill, reconciliation and cutover; naive dual writes can diverge).
3. **Cost**: what grows fastest on the bill and how to contain it.
4. **Operability**: how you'll find the next bottleneck before users do.

The lesson's staff bar adds evolution, operability, cost and organisational trade-offs on top of a working design.

lessons.title: Design a URL shortener
lessons.summary: Design a TinyURL/Bitly-style service, focusing on short-code generation (hashing, counters, Snowflake), 301 vs 302 redirects, caching and click analytics.
lessons.body:
A URL shortener looks trivial: map a short code to a long URL. That's why it's a favourite opener. The interviewer isn't interested in the mapping; they want to see how you generate billions of unique short codes without a bottleneck, how you serve a very read-heavy workload, and what you do about analytics.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Create a short link from a long URL. Returns something like `https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x`.
- Visiting a short link redirects to the original URL.
- Optional custom alias (`sho.rt/summer-sale`).
- Optional expiry.
- Link owners can see click counts (by day, country, referrer).

**Non-functional**

- Very read-heavy: assume 10 redirects for every link created.
- Low latency redirects: p99 under ~50 ms server-side.
- Highly available: a broken redirect breaks someone else's website, email or printed poster.
- Durable: a created link must never be lost or remapped.
- Avoid exposing sequential allocation through codes. Truly private links require authorization: at 10% namespace occupancy, a random probe finds some valid code about once in ten attempts, regardless of the permutation.

Out of scope: user management, billing, link editing UI.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume **100 million new links per day** and a **10:1** read:write ratio.

```
Writes: 100M / 10^5 s    ≈ 1,000/s
        (peak x3)        ≈ 3,000/s
Reads:  1B / 10^5 s      ≈ 10,000/s
        (peak x3)        ≈ 30,000/s
```

Storage, keeping links for 10 years at about 500 bytes each (long URL, code, owner, timestamps):

```
Links: 100M x 365 x 10  ≈ 365 billion
Size:  365B x 500 B     ≈ 180 TB
With 3x replication     ≈ 550 TB
```

How long must the code be? Using **base62** (`a–z`, `A–Z`, `0–9`):

| Length | Codes |
|---|---|
| 6 | 62^6 ≈ 57 billion |
| 7 | 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion |
| 8 | 62^8 ≈ 218 trillion |

Six characters would run out in about 1.5 years. **Seven** gives 3.5 trillion, about ten times our 10-year need. That headroom matters for one of the ID strategies below.

Cache sizing using the 80/20 rule: if 20% of links get most of the traffic, suppose the chosen hot set contains 200 million distinct links. At 500 B each its raw payload is 100 GB, before cache overhead and replication. The 80/20 rule and a billion daily requests do not determine the number of distinct hot links; estimate that from access traces and the desired hit rate.

The cache hit rate then sets the database read load. At a 90% hit rate, 30,000 peak redirects/s leaves about 3,000 reads/s for the store; at 99%, only 300. Link popularity is heavily skewed (most links are clicked mostly in the first days after being shared), so high hit rates are realistic.

What the numbers tell us: writes are modest, reads are high but cache well, and storage (180 TB raw, over half a petabyte replicated) motivates evaluating horizontal partitioning, storage tiers and recovery costs; raw size alone does not prove a universal single-node limit.

## Step 3: API

```
POST /v1/links
  {longUrl, customAlias?, expiresAt?}
  -> 201 {code, shortUrl}

GET /{code}
  -> 302 Location: <longUrl>
  -> 404 if unknown or expired

GET /v1/links/{code}/stats?from&to
  -> {clicks, byCountry, byReferrer}
```

The create endpoint takes an API key and is rate limited per key (spammers love shorteners). It should accept an `Idempotency-Key` header so a retried request doesn't create two links.

## Step 4: Data model

The core access pattern is a point lookup: **code → long URL**. No joins, no range scans. That suits a key-value or wide-column store partitioned by `code`: DynamoDB, Cassandra, or a sharded MySQL/Postgres with `code` as the shard key.

```
links
  code        PK  (7-char string)
  long_url        (up to ~2 KB)
  owner_id
  created_at
  expires_at      (nullable)
```

Owners also want "list my links", which is a different access pattern (by `owner_id`). Handle it with a secondary index (a DynamoDB GSI) or a separate `links_by_owner` table, rather than scanning.

Analytics data is a completely different shape (high-volume, append-only, aggregated) and lives elsewhere.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
        Client
          |
          v
   CDN / load balancer
          |
     +----+------+
     v           v
 Write API    Redirect svc
     |           |      \
     v           v       v
 ID allocator  Redis   Kafka
     |           |    (clicks)
     v           v       |
   Links store <-+       v
   (KV, sharded)     Analytics
                     (OLAP)
```

**Create**: the write API validates the URL (and checks an appropriate threat-intelligence service under its usage terms; Google Safe Browsing is limited to non-commercial use, while commercial users are directed to Web Risk), obtains a unique code, writes `code → long_url` to the links store, and returns.

**Redirect**: the redirect service looks up the code in Redis; on a miss it reads the store and populates the cache. It returns a redirect and fires a click event to Kafka *asynchronously*, with bounded buffers and an explicit drop/backpressure policy so analytics do not block redirect completion.

Read and write paths are separate services because they scale very differently: 30k reads/s vs 3k writes/s, with different latency targets.

## Deep dive 1: Generating short codes

This is the heart of the problem. You need billions of unique, short, ideally unguessable codes, generated by many servers without a global lock.

### Option A: Hash the long URL

Hash the URL with SHA-256 and map it approximately uniformly into the base62 code space. The collision arithmetic below assumes uniform codes; naively taking leading digits of a variable-width integer encoding can introduce bias.

- **Pro**: stateless; any server can compute it.
- **Con: collisions.** Truncating to 7 characters leaves a 3.5-trillion space. By the [birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem), collisions become likely after about √(3.5T) ≈ 1.9 million links. With hundreds of billions of links you will collide constantly, so every write needs an atomic insert-if-absent and a retry on conflict (for example, appending a counter and rehashing).
- **Con: same URL, same code.** Two users shortening the same URL get the same link, which breaks per-owner analytics and expiry. You can salt with the user ID, but then you lose the dedup that was the main appeal.

### Option B: A counter, base62-encoded

Give each link the next integer and base62-encode it. With the alphabet ordered `0–9`, `a–z`, `A–Z`: `1 → "1"`, `125 → "21"` (2 × 62 + 1), and 62^7 − 1 (about 3.5 trillion) → `"ZZZZZZZ"`, the largest 7-character code.

- **Pro**: no collisions, ever. Codes are as short as possible.
- **Con**: a single global counter is a bottleneck and single point of failure.
- **Fix: range allocation.** A coordination service (a small database table, ZooKeeper or etcd) hands each write server a *block* of, say, 1 million IDs. The server allocates from its block in memory and only goes back for a new block when it runs out. At 3,000 writes/s, the coordinator is contacted once every few minutes. If a server crashes, the rest of its block is simply wasted. With 3.5 trillion codes, wasting millions is irrelevant.
- **Con: guessable.** Sequential codes let anyone enumerate links (`aaaaaab`, `aaaaaac`...). Fix this by passing the counter through a reversible permutation before encoding: for example, multiply by a large constant that shares no factor with 62^7 (so not a multiple of 2 or 31) modulo 62^7, or use a small Feistel network keyed with a secret. It stays collision-free (it's a bijection) but looks random. The multiplication trick only hides the pattern from casual eyes (two known codes reveal the constant); a vetted keyed permutation can hide sequence relationships, but a custom small Feistel construction is not established as secure here.

### Option C: Snowflake-style IDs

[Snowflake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID), from Twitter, packs a 64-bit ID as:

```
| 1 | 41 bits ms | 10 bits  | 12 bits |
|   | timestamp  | machine  | seq     |
```

Each worker has 4,096 sequence values per millisecond. Generation avoids per-ID coordination, but worker IDs must be assigned uniquely and restart/clock behavior must prevent reuse.

- **Pro**: fully decentralised, roughly time-ordered.
- **Con: length.** A Snowflake ID uses 63 bits, and today's values are around 10^18, which takes **11 base62 characters**, not 7. For a *short*ener, that's a real cost.
- **Con: clocks.** If a machine's clock goes backwards (NTP correction), it can reissue IDs unless the generator refuses to run until the clock catches up.

### Option D: Pre-generated key service

A key generation service pre-computes random 7-character codes, stores them in an "unused" table, and hands batches to write servers. It's essentially Option B with random rather than sequential codes. It works, but you have to store and manage billions of unused keys.

> [!tip] Recommended answer
> Range-allocated counters with a bijective shuffle, base62-encoded to 7 characters. Collision-free and short when ranges are never reused; the shuffle is not an access-control mechanism, and the coordinator is touched only once per million links.

**Custom aliases** go in the same table using a conditional write ("insert if not exists": DynamoDB `attribute_not_exists`, or a primary key constraint in SQL). To stop a custom alias colliding with a future generated code, either reserve a distinct format for aliases (for example, require them to be 8+ characters or contain a hyphen) or have the generator skip codes that already exist.

## Deep dive 2: 301 vs 302

Both send the browser to the long URL. The difference is caching.

| | 301 Permanent | 302 Found |
|---|---|---|
| Heuristic cacheability | Yes | Not normally; explicit freshness can permit storage |
| Later clicks hit us? | Depends on freshness policy | Depends on freshness policy |
| Analytics | Cached visits may be missed | Cached visits may be missed |
| Updated target seen? | Depends on cache policy | Depends on cache policy |

A fresh cached redirect can bypass your service, hiding visits and delaying target or expiry changes. A **301** is heuristically cacheable; **302/307** can also be cached with explicit freshness. Use an explicit policy such as `Cache-Control: no-store` when repeat navigation should resolve through your service, and account for analytics delivery failures separately.

Without explicit cache headers, browsers treat a 301 as cacheable and may keep it indefinitely; a 302 is cached only if headers say so. A permanent redirect can still use a short freshness lifetime or `no-store`; the status and cache policy serve different purposes.

> [!note] Content gap: live provider headers
> Exact Bitly, t.co and TinyURL cache-header claims have been removed. No reproducible set of representative URLs and dated response captures was supplied, so this audit cannot reliably present those variable deployment settings as provider-wide facts.

So the real lever is `Cache-Control`, not only the status code. Say the trade-off explicitly; that's what the interviewer is checking.

## Deep dive 3: Analytics

Never update a counter row synchronously on every redirect. At 30,000 redirects/s, a popular link would become a hot row and add latency to every redirect.

Instead:

1. The redirect service emits a click event (`code, timestamp, country from IP, user agent, referrer`) to Kafka, fire-and-forget, and returns immediately.
2. A stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) aggregates events into per-link, per-hour buckets.
3. Aggregates go into an OLAP store such as ClickHouse or Druid, which answers "clicks by country last 7 days" quickly.

Raw events can also be written to object storage (S3) for reprocessing. If Kafka is briefly unavailable, the redirect must still work: buffer locally and drop analytics before you ever fail a redirect. Redirects are the product; analytics are a feature.

## Deep dive 4: Caching and expiry

The application uses cache-aside: check Redis, read the store on a miss, then populate Redis. Links are effectively immutable, so cache invalidation is easy; set a TTL (say, 24 hours) and evict on expiry or deletion.

Two subtleties:

- **Negative caching.** Bots hammer random codes. Cache "not found" for a short time (60 s) so they don't all fall through to the database. A Bloom filter can reject absent codes only when it covers all committed codes relevant to that read; a stale filter must not suppress fresh links.
- **Expiry.** Check `expires_at` on every read (lazy expiry), and let a background job or the store's TTL feature (DynamoDB TTL, Cassandra TTL) physically delete rows later.

## Deep dive 5: Consistency after create

A subtle bug lurks between negative caching and replication. A user creates a link and pastes it into a chat; a friend clicks within 200 ms. If the redirect hits a replica (or another region) that hasn't received the write yet, it returns 404 and *caches the 404 for 60 seconds*. The link looks broken for a minute.

Fixes, roughly in order of preference:

- **Write-through on create.** The write API puts `code → long_url` into the cache as it writes the store, and deletes any negative entry for that code.
- **Fall back to the primary on a miss.** If the replica says "not found", retry against the primary (or home region) before caching a negative result. Misses on real codes are rare, so the extra cost is small.
- **Keep negative TTLs short** (seconds, not minutes) and only negatively cache codes that fail a cheap format or Bloom filter check.

Immutable mappings simplify replication, but deletion, expiry, abuse blocking, custom-alias uniqueness and stale negative-cache fills still need consistency rules. A create racing with an older miss can be overwritten by a late negative fill; version or condition cache writes, or avoid negative caching valid-looking codes when strict freshness is required.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Hot links**: a viral link can get 100k+ requests/s, more than a single Redis shard wants. Add a small in-process cache on each redirect server, or serve the redirect from the CDN edge.
- **ID coordinator**: range allocation makes it nearly irrelevant, but run it replicated (etcd/ZooKeeper) so block allocation survives a node loss.
- **Abuse**: shorteners are used to hide phishing links. Scan on creation, rescan periodically, and be able to disable a link globally (another reason to keep browser caching of redirects short).

## At 10x scale

At 1 billion new links a day and 300k redirects/s:

- **Seven characters is no longer enough** for 10 years (3.65 trillion links vs 3.5 trillion codes). Move to 8 characters (218 trillion) for new links. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so new generated links use exactly eight characters (left-pad short encodings), with a fresh permutation over [0, 62^8). Also revise alias reservations or atomically skip already-claimed aliases.
- **Storage reaches petabytes** (about 1.8 PB raw over 10 years). Expire links nobody has clicked for years, or move them to cheaper storage.
- **Go multi-region.** Redirects are read-only and links are immutable, so replicate the links store asynchronously to every region and serve redirects locally. Give each region its own ID ranges so regions never need to coordinate on writes. A link created in Europe might take a second to resolve in Asia; the primary-fallback from deep dive 5 covers that window.
- **Push redirects to the edge.** CDN workers (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) can hold hot mappings and reduce origin work; end-to-end latency still needs measurement, shipping click logs back in batches.
- **Shard the analytics pipeline** by code and pre-aggregate at the edge before sending upstream.

## Key takeaways

- Seven base62 characters give 3.5 trillion codes; size the code length from your 10-year link count.
- Hashing needs collision checks (birthday bound ≈ √N), counters need coordination, Snowflake IDs are too long for a shortener.
- Non-reused range allocations plus a bijective shuffle avoid collisions; private links still need authorization.
- Redirect caching trades origin load against freshness and click visibility. `Cache-Control` matters for both 301 and 302; choose it explicitly.
- Cache hit rate sets database load; negative caching requires race-safe fills and fresh source/filter checks to avoid hiding newly created links.
- Emit clicks asynchronously to a log and aggregate in a stream processor; never block a redirect on analytics.
- Links are immutable, so caching, multi-region replication and edge serving are all easy wins.

## Further reading

- [URL shortening (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URL_shortening)
- [Snowflake ID (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID)
- [MDN: 301 Moved Permanently](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301)
- [MDN: 302 Found](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/302)
- [System Design Primer: design Pastebin / Bit.ly](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer/blob/master/solutions/system_design/pastebin/README.md)
- [Hello Interview: design a URL shortener like Bit.ly](https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/bitly)
- [Base62 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base62)

questions.prompt: You expect to create **50 billion** short links over the life of the service. What is the shortest base62 code length that can hold them all with at least twice the required namespace capacity?

options.text: 7 characters
options.explanation: Correct. 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, about 70x the requirement. That headroom tolerates wasted ID ranges, reserved formats and growth beyond the forecast.

options.text: 6 characters
options.explanation: Wrong. 62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion, barely above 50 billion. At 50 billion allocated codes you would be about 88% full; waste or further growth could exhaust the remaining space.

options.text: 5 characters
options.explanation: Wrong. 62^5 ≈ 916 million codes, which is less than 2% of what you need.

options.text: 11 characters
options.explanation: Wrong. 11 characters is what a 64-bit Snowflake ID needs, giving ~5 × 10^19 codes. It works but makes links needlessly long for a service whose whole point is shortness.

questions.workedExample:
Compute powers of 62:

```
62^5 ≈ 9.2 x 10^8   (916 million)
62^6 ≈ 5.7 x 10^10  (56.8 billion)
62^7 ≈ 3.5 x 10^12  (3.5 trillion)
```

Compare with 5 × 10^10 needed. Six characters gives a ratio of only 1.1x; seven gives 70x. You want headroom because range allocation wastes IDs when servers crash, and forecasts are usually wrong, so choose **7**.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes generating codes by taking the first 7 base62 characters of `SHA-256(longUrl)`. The service will hold hundreds of billions of links. What is the main problem?

options.text: SHA-256 is too slow to compute at 3,000 writes per second.
options.explanation: Wrong. No hardware benchmark is supplied; the demonstrated problem is namespace collisions, not an established hashing bottleneck.

options.text: Hash-based codes can't be stored in a key-value store.
options.explanation: Wrong. A hash-derived code is just a string key; any KV store handles it. The issue is uniqueness, not storage.

options.text: Truncated hashes collide frequently at this scale, so every write needs an existence check and retry, and identical URLs from different users map to the same code.
options.explanation: Correct. With a 3.5-trillion space, the birthday bound puts a 50% chance of at least one collision at ~2.2 million links. At hundreds of billions, a meaningful fraction of new inserts will collide, and dedup by URL breaks per-user ownership, expiry and analytics.

options.text: Hashes are reversible, so attackers can recover the long URL from the code.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cryptographic hashes are one-way, and truncating makes reversal even less possible. Predictable input URLs can still be guessed and hashed, and a densely occupied short namespace can be probed.

questions.workedExample:
Apply the birthday problem. For a space of N codes, a 50% collision chance arrives at about `1.18 × √N` items.

```
N = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 x 10^12
√N ≈ 1.87 x 10^6
50% point ≈ 2.2 million links
```

Once you hold, say, 350 billion links, the chance that a fresh random 7-char code is already taken is `350B / 3.5T = 10%`. So one write in ten collides and needs a retry, each requiring an atomic conditional insert, not a racy read-before-write. Add the dedup problem (same URL → same code for every user) and a counter-based scheme is much simpler.

questions.prompt: Your product manager wants accurate click counts and the ability to disable malicious links instantly. Which redirect status should the service return?

options.text: 301 Moved Permanently, because it is the standard for URL redirects.
options.explanation: Wrong as stated. Without cache headers, browsers may cache a 301 indefinitely, so repeat clicks never reach you and you can't reliably disable the link. Provider-wide header claims require current representative response captures, which are not supplied.

options.text: 404 Not Found, then let the browser search for the URL.
options.explanation: Wrong. 404 means the resource doesn't exist. It would break every link.

options.text: 200 OK with a page containing a JavaScript redirect.
options.explanation: Wrong. It works, but adds a full page load, breaks non-browser clients (curl, bots, some email clients) and harms SEO. Use a proper HTTP redirect.

options.text: 302 Found (or 307) with Cache-Control: no-store; enforce blocking on the redirect path and measure analytics delivery separately.
options.explanation: Correct. Explicit no-store avoids retaining this redirect in compliant HTTP caches. It does not revoke already-resolved destinations, guarantee click-event delivery, or instantly invalidate your own cache layers.

questions.workedExample: Choose an explicit cache policy. A 301 is heuristically cacheable; temporary redirects can also be cached with explicit freshness. For the stated control requirement, use 302/307 with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and make origin/edge blocking checks sufficiently fresh. Requests already redirected cannot be recalled. Click analytics also need delivery, deduplication and bot-counting rules; HTTP status alone cannot guarantee accurate counts. Exact provider cache settings are omitted because no reproducible dated captures are available.

questions.prompt: You use range allocation: a coordinator hands each write server a block of **1,000,000** IDs. Peak write rate is **3,000 links/s** across 10 servers. Roughly how often does the coordinator receive a block request, and what happens if a server crashes mid-block?

options.text: About 3,000 times per second; the crash corrupts the counter.
options.explanation: Wrong. That would be the rate with no batching at all. With 1M-ID blocks the coordinator is consulted once per million IDs, and a crash cannot corrupt a counter that has already moved past the block.

options.text: About once every 5–6 minutes in total; the unused IDs in the crashed server's block are simply skipped.
options.explanation: Correct. 1M / 3,000 ≈ 333 s between block requests overall. Unused IDs are wasted, but with 3.5 trillion codes, losing a million per crash is negligible, and no ID is ever issued twice.

options.text: About once per day; the crashed block is reassigned to another server.
options.explanation: Wrong on both counts. At 3,000/s you consume 1M IDs in ~5.5 minutes, not a day. Reassigning a partially used block is dangerous because you don't know which IDs were already issued.

options.text: Never; each server generates IDs from its own clock.
options.explanation: Wrong. That describes Snowflake-style generation, which needs no coordinator, not range allocation.

questions.workedExample:
```
IDs per block:         1,000,000
Global write rate:     3,000/s
Time to use 1 block:   1M / 3k ≈ 333 s
```

So the coordinator handles roughly one request every ~5.5 minutes in aggregate (each of 10 servers asks about once an hour). That's why it isn't a bottleneck.

On a crash, the coordinator has already advanced past the block, so the remaining IDs are never handed out again. Waste per crash ≤ 1M; even 1,000 crashes waste 1 billion, under 0.03% of 62^7.

questions.prompt: A usability review flags that your counter-based codes are sequential: `aZ3kQ9x` is followed by `aZ3kQ9y`, revealing sequential allocation. Private-link access control is handled separately. What algebraic approach that keeps codes collision-free and 7 characters long?

options.text: Switch to random 7-character codes and retry on collision.
options.explanation: Partly works but reintroduces the collision problem: at 10% fill, one write in ten collides and needs a read-before-write retry. You've traded a security problem for a correctness and latency one.

options.text: Use Snowflake IDs instead.
options.explanation: Wrong. Snowflake IDs are also time-ordered and largely predictable (timestamp plus machine plus sequence), and they need about 11 base62 characters, breaking the 7-character requirement.

options.text: Apply a bijective permutation to the counter (e.g. multiply by a constant coprime with 62^7, mod 62^7, with the explicit understanding that this multiplication is only obfuscation) before base62-encoding.
options.explanation: Correct. A bijection on [0, 62^7) maps each counter value to a unique code, so it stays collision-free, but consecutive counters produce unrelated-looking codes. This guarantees uniqueness, not secrecy: at 10% occupancy random probes hit valid links about 10% of the time.

options.text: Rate limit the redirect endpoint so enumeration takes longer.
options.explanation: Wrong as the main fix. Rate limiting slows a single attacker, but distributed scrapers bypass it easily. It's a useful defence in depth, not a substitute for unpredictable codes.

questions.workedExample:
You want a function `f` such that:

1. `f` is one-to-one on [0, 62^7), so no collisions.
2. `f(n)` and `f(n+1)` look unrelated.

Simplest version: choose a constant `a` coprime with 62^7 (any odd number not divisible by 31 works, since 62 = 2 × 31). Then `f(n) = (a × n) mod 62^7` is a bijection, though two known codes reveal `a`. A custom four-round Feistel recipe is omitted because no reviewed cryptographic construction is supplied. For private links use authorization or a properly designed longer capability token; a dense seven-character namespace is not adequate secrecy.

```
1000001 -> f -> base62 -> "Qx81bKa"
1000002 -> f -> base62 -> "3mPz0Wd"
```

Codes remain unique and 7 characters, with no extra database reads.

questions.prompt: The redirect path must hold **p99 under 50 ms at 30,000 req/s** while also recording click analytics. Which design choices help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Publish a click event to Kafka asynchronously and return the redirect without waiting for the acknowledgement.
options.explanation: Correct. Decoupling analytics from the request path means the redirect's latency depends only on the lookup. If Kafka is slow, buffer or drop events rather than delay redirects.

options.text: Increment a `click_count` column in the links table on every redirect.
options.explanation: Incorrect. A synchronous write per redirect adds latency and creates hot rows for viral links, causing lock contention exactly when traffic is highest.

options.text: Read-through cache in Redis plus a short-lived negative cache for unknown codes.
options.explanation: Correct. Most lookups hit memory, and negative caching stops bots probing random codes from falling through to the database.

options.text: A small in-process LRU cache on each redirect server for the hottest links.
options.explanation: Correct. It avoids a network hop for viral links and protects the Redis shard that owns a hot key from saturating.

options.text: Use a 2PC transaction across the links store and the analytics store so both are always consistent.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Two-phase commit adds multiple round trips and blocks on the slowest participant. Analytics can be eventually consistent; a redirect must not wait on it.

questions.workedExample:
Budget the 50 ms:

| Step | Illustrative latency input, not a benchmark |
|---|---|
| In-process cache hit | < 0.1 ms |
| Redis hit | ~0.5–1 ms |
| KV store read | ~5–10 ms |
| Sync DB write | +5–20 ms, worse under contention |

Keep only reads on the critical path and push every write (analytics) off it. Layered caches handle hot keys; negative caching handles bots. Synchronous work can increase latency and contention; whether it violates 50 ms needs a representative load test.

questions.prompt: Traffic grows 10x to **1 billion new links/day**, kept for 10 years, with 7-character codes. Which hard namespace-capacity problem follows directly from these numbers?

options.text: The ID coordinator can no longer keep up with block requests.
options.explanation: Wrong. At 1B links/day the peak is about 30,000 writes/s, so 1M-ID blocks are requested about 0.03 times a second, roughly once every 33 s overall. You can also simply make blocks bigger.

options.text: Base62 encoding becomes too CPU-intensive.
options.explanation: Wrong. Encoding takes a bounded number of divisions here; no measured CPU limit is supplied.

options.text: Redis can't hold the hot set.
options.explanation: Daily request count does not specify the number of distinct hot keys or their memory footprint. Trace the working set and benchmark capacity; no fixed 1 TB hot set follows from this prompt.

options.text: The 7-character code space runs out: 3.65 trillion links needed vs ~3.5 trillion codes available.
options.explanation: Correct. 1B × 365 × 10 = 3.65 × 10^12, slightly more than 62^7 ≈ 3.52 × 10^12, before counting wasted ranges. You need to move new links to 8 characters (218 trillion).

questions.workedExample:
Recompute the key estimate with the new numbers:

```
Links in 10 years = 1B/day x 365 x 10
                  = 3.65 x 10^12
Code space (7)    = 62^7 ≈ 3.52 x 10^12
```

You'd exhaust 7-character codes in about 9.6 years, sooner with waste. Moving to 8 characters gives 62^8 ≈ 2.18 × 10^14, about 60x headroom. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so you can switch with no migration: new generated links use exactly eight characters, including left-padding, and old codes keep working. Revise alias rules or use conditional inserts because existing custom aliases may already have eight characters.

The lesson: always re-run your capacity maths when the scale changes; a constraint that was 10x away can become binding.

questions.prompt: Peak redirect traffic is **30,000 req/s**. Your Redis cache hit rate is **95%**. A teammate wants to cut database cost by lowering the cache TTL, which drops the hit rate to **80%**. How does the database read load change?

options.text: From 1,500 to 6,000 reads/s: four times as much.
options.explanation: Correct. Misses are what reach the database: 5% of 30k = 1,500/s, and 20% of 30k = 6,000/s. A 15-point drop in hit rate quadruples database load.

options.text: From 28,500 to 24,000 reads/s: slightly less.
options.explanation: Wrong. Those are the cache hits, not the database reads. The database only sees misses.

options.text: It barely changes, because the hit rate fell by only 15%.
options.explanation: Wrong. Think in miss rate, not hit rate: misses go from 5% to 20%, a 4x increase.

options.text: From 1,500 to 1,800 reads/s, because only the extra 15% of hits are lost.
options.explanation: Wrong. 15% of 30,000 is 4,500 extra misses per second, not 300.

questions.workedExample:
Database load = total × miss rate.

```
95% hit: 30,000 x 0.05 = 1,500/s
80% hit: 30,000 x 0.20 = 6,000/s
```

The miss rate is what matters, and it is very sensitive near the top: going from 99% to 98% hit rate *doubles* database load. Long TTLs save reads but can delay deletion or abuse blocking unless those states have a separate freshness mechanism. Choose the cache policy against both cost and correctness requirements.

questions.prompt: Users report that links they've *just* created sometimes 404 for about a minute, then start working. Redirects read from async replicas, and unknown codes are negatively cached for 60 s. What is happening, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The ID allocator is issuing duplicate codes; switch to Snowflake IDs.
options.explanation: Wrong. Duplicates would cause wrong redirects that never heal, not a 404 that fixes itself after a minute.

options.text: A click arrives before the replica has the new row, the 404 is negatively cached for 60 s, so the link looks broken until that entry expires. Write the mapping into the cache on create (clearing any negative entry), and check the primary before caching a 'not found'.
options.explanation: Correct. The 60-second healing time matches the negative-cache TTL, which is the giveaway. Write-through on create plus a primary fallback on a miss helps, but requires conditional/versioned cache fills so an older miss cannot overwrite the freshly created mapping.

options.text: Browsers cached a 301 for the old URL; switch to 302.
options.explanation: Wrong. The link is new, so no browser can have a cached redirect for it. The 404 comes from your own service.

options.text: Turn off negative caching altogether.
options.explanation: Partly works but overcorrects. Bots probing random codes would then all fall through to the database. Keep negative caching, but stop it caching false negatives for fresh links.

questions.workedExample:
Reconstruct the timeline:

```
t=0     create -> primary
t=50ms  click -> replica: no row
        cache 'not found' 60 s
t=200ms replica receives row
t=60s   negative entry expires
```

Two ingredients help; neither alone proves correctness against all concurrent cache-fill races:

1. **Write-through on create**: set `code → url` in Redis and delete any negative key.
2. **Primary fallback**: on a replica miss, ask the primary before caching a negative result.

In interviews, linking a symptom's duration to a specific TTL is a strong debugging signal.

questions.prompt: You're adding **custom aliases** (`sho.rt/summer-sale`) to a service that also issues generated 7-character codes from a counter. Which measures are needed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insert the alias with a conditional write (insert-if-not-exists, or a primary key constraint), so two users racing for the same alias can't both win.
options.explanation: Correct. A check-then-insert has a race window; the conditional write makes the store the arbiter, and the loser gets a clear 'alias taken' error.

options.text: Stop custom aliases from ever matching a future generated code, e.g. require 8+ characters or a hyphen, or have the generator skip taken codes.
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise someone can claim `aZ3kQ9x` today and the counter later produces it, causing a conflict on an automatic write that no user can resolve.

options.text: Block reserved and abusive words such as `api`, `login`, `admin` and brand names.
options.explanation: Correct. Aliases that look like your own paths or impersonate brands are a phishing and routing risk. A denylist on creation is cheap.

options.text: Store custom aliases in a separate database so they can't collide.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The redirect path still has to look up one namespace. Two stores means two lookups per redirect and doesn't remove the collision; it hides it.

options.text: Hash the alias with SHA-256 before storing it.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The alias is the key users type. Hashing it adds nothing and makes listing and support harder.

questions.workedExample:
Aliases share one namespace with generated codes, so three things can go wrong:

1. **Two users race** for the same alias → conditional write.
2. **Alias vs future generated code** → disjoint formats (aliases ≥ 8 chars or contain `-`), so the generator can never produce one.
3. **Abuse** → denylist reserved paths and brand names.

A single table keyed by `code` keeps the redirect path to one lookup.

questions.prompt: A link in a Super Bowl advert gets **200,000 clicks/s** for ten minutes. It lives on one Redis shard that handles about 100k ops/s. Analytics for the advertiser matter. What is the best mitigation?

options.text: Re-shard Redis with more nodes so the key gets more capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. Consistent hashing still places one key on one shard, so adding nodes doesn't spread a single hot key.

options.text: Return a 301 with no cache headers so browsers stop coming back.
options.explanation: Wrong for this case. Each viewer clicks once, so browser caching saves little, and you'd lose control of the link. Most of the 200k/s are different people.

options.text: Serve the redirect from the CDN edge or an in-process cache on every redirect server with a short TTL, and emit click events from there in batches.
options.explanation: Correct. Spreading the read across hundreds of edge locations or app servers takes it off the single shard, and a short TTL (seconds) keeps control. Batched click logs preserve analytics.

options.text: Rate limit the link to 100k clicks/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. Dropping half the advertiser's traffic during their most expensive minute is the worst possible outcome.

questions.workedExample:
The bottleneck is one key on one shard, so the fix must **replicate the read**, not partition it further.

```
Edge/in-process copies: hundreds
Load per copy: 200k / 300 ≈ 700/s
TTL 5 s: nominal cache freshness 5 s
```

Analytics can survive if batches are durably buffered/retried and duplicates handled; best-effort buffering can still lose events. In this design, edge workers or app servers log each click locally and ship counts in batches, rather than writing per click. The same idea (replicate hot keys, batch writes) applies to every hot-key question in this module.

questions.prompt: You expand to three regions so redirects are served locally. Generated-code link creation must remain available during a bounded partition while preallocated ID ranges remain; globally unique custom aliases are out of scope. Which choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give each region its own pre-allocated ID ranges, so regions generate codes without talking to each other.
options.explanation: Correct. Disjoint ranges guarantee uniqueness with no cross-region coordination, so a partitioned region can still create links.

options.text: Replicate the links table asynchronously to all regions.
options.explanation: Correct. Links are written once and never updated, so there are no conflicting writes to merge. Async replication keeps create latency local.

options.text: On a local miss, check the link's home region before returning 404.
options.explanation: Correct. It covers replication lag only when the home region is reachable; it cannot resolve an unknown link during that region's isolation. The home region can be encoded in the ID range, so you know where to ask.

options.text: Use a single global counter with synchronous cross-region consensus for every create.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each create would pay a cross-region round trip (~100 ms), and a partitioned region couldn't create links at all, breaking the requirement.

options.text: Use 301 with an infinite cache so other regions are rarely asked.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It doesn't help create availability, and it gives up analytics and the ability to disable abusive links.

questions.workedExample:
Immutability is what makes this easy:

1. **Uniqueness without coordination**: region-specific ID ranges.
2. **Replication without conflicts**: rows never change, so last-writer-wins issues don't arise.
3. **Lag handling**: fall back to the home region on a miss.

Avoid putting anything cross-region and synchronous on the create path: it adds deployment-dependent network latency and may be unavailable in an isolated region. Disabling or deleting links still requires propagation rules even when destination mappings are immutable.
